text:
Both responses define the p-value correctly as the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Both list the main misconceptions accurately, including that a p-value is not the probability the null is true, not the probability of replication, and not effect size. Both fit under 120 words.

Response A adds two points that carry real reasoning. It warns that p > 0.05 does not mean "no effect," which is one of the most common misreadings. It also notes that a p-value cannot give the probability of a hypothesis without prior information. Response B's final bullet, that a p-value is not evidence the alternative is true with a given confidence, covers part of this, but less directly. Response B is cleaner and more concise, but its extra brevity drops the caveats that matter most. Response A's extra words add correct and useful content, so it is somewhat better.

Verdict: A
